If your L-39 jet is going down, you pull one double handle at the front of your seat.
First, small explosive charges blow the canopy away.
Then a powder charge fires the seat up its rails, and a rocket under the seat lifts you higher.
The kick can reach seventeen g.
A tiny stabilizing chute keeps the seat from tumbling.
Then the seat falls away, and a big main parachute lowers you at about six meters per second.
But it only works within limits.
On the ground, the jet must be doing at least one hundred fifty kilometers per hour, so the canopy clears properly.
In a spin, the manual says to eject before fifteen hundred meters.
And with two pilots, a blocking system stops both seats firing at once, so they can't collide.
So one pull starts a chain reaction that ends with you hanging safely under a parachute.
